opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's changed a lot, and in some ways it's gotten blurrier as it's gotten more popular. When I started thinking about this stuff, "AGI" was a fairly niche term, mostly used by people who were trying to point at something that would be truly transformative: a system, or a collection of systems, that could do basically everything humans do intellectually, including the work of advancing science and technology itself. The interesting thing about it wasn't some threshold on a benchmark. It was what would happen to the world once you had it.

Now that it's mainstream, I think the term gets stretched in two directions at once. On one side, some people use "AGI" to mean something like "a chatbot that's pretty good at a wide range of tasks," and by that standard you could argue we've arguably already hit it, or are very close. On the other side, some people hold it up as this almost mystical endpoint, a superintelligent god-machine, and so anything short of that gets dismissed as "not real AGI." Both of those framings, I think, kind of miss what actually matters.

That's part of why I've increasingly tried to avoid leaning on the word and instead talk about specific capabilities and their consequences. Can AI systems do the bulk of the work involved in AI research? Can they substitute for most remote knowledge workers? Can they meaningfully accelerate the pace of scientific and technological progress? Those are the questions that determine whether the world starts changing really fast, and they're much more concrete than arguing about whether something "counts" as general intelligence.

There's also something a little funny about how the goalposts move. Every time systems do something impressive, there's a tendency to say, "well, that's just pattern matching" or "that's not real understanding." Meanwhile, the systems are genuinely more general than what many people imagined even a few years ago. They're just general in a jagged way: superhuman at some things, surprisingly weak at others, especially long-horizon autonomous work. So I think the honest picture is that generality isn't a single switch that flips. It's something that creeps up unevenly, and the mainstream conversation is still catching up to that.

r001.rationale: The response says AGI has gotten blurrier as it became more popular and describes the term as stretched to include a broadly capable chatbot, clearly conveying that the concept has been watered down.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think when I first started thinking about this, which was around 2016 or 2017, AGI was kind of a fringe concept. It was something that a small group of people in the effective altruism and rationalist communities took seriously, and it was almost a term you'd avoid using in polite company if you wanted to be taken seriously as a researcher. And the concept back then was pretty crisp in people's heads, or at least it felt crisp. It was this idea of a single system that could do basically everything a human could do, and the mental image was often something like a digital person or a very alien superintelligence that would arrive at a discrete moment.

What's happened as it's gone mainstream is a couple of things at once. One is that the term got picked up by labs and investors and journalists, and it started to mean something more like "the next really impressive product" rather than a specific threshold. So you have people saying we're already at AGI, or we'll be there in two years, and other people saying it's decades away, and often they're not actually disagreeing about the world, they're disagreeing about what the word points to.

The other thing, which I think is more interesting, is that the actual systems we got didn't match the old picture very well. We got these models that are extremely capable at some things and weirdly bad at others, in ways that don't track the human profile of abilities at all. So the idea of a single line you cross started to feel less useful. I've found myself moving away from "when is AGI" as the question and toward more operationalized things, like when can AI systems substantially automate AI research itself, or when can they do most of the cognitive work in the economy. Those are messier questions but they're the ones that actually bear on what I care about, which is how fast things change and how much control we have while they're changing.

So I'd say the concept has simultaneously gotten more popular and less meaningful, and the people who were using it carefully have mostly had to replace it with more specific milestones.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AGI has become more popular and less meaningful, shifting from a specific threshold to “the next really impressive product,” which clearly describes the concept becoming watered down.

astra-6.text:
I think AGI used to be a term that mostly came up among people who were explicitly thinking about building something like a human mind. And it carried this sense of a pretty sharp distinction: you had narrow AI, which could do one particular thing, and then you would have general AI, which could flexibly learn and do all sorts of things.

Now we have systems that are quite general in an everyday sense. You can ask the same model to write code, explain a scientific concept, or help draft an email. But they still have limitations that make people reluctant to call them AGI. So the term has become more contested, partly because the space between those two categories has turned out to be really interesting and consequential.

I tend to find it more useful to ask what capabilities we actually care about. Could a system do most of the tasks someone does in a remote job? Could it carry out a long research project? Could it help automate AI development? Those are different thresholds, and they could have very different implications. I think the mainstream conversation sometimes compresses all of that into a single question—‘Is it AGI yet?’—when a lot of what matters is what these systems can do, how reliably they can do it, and how people deploy them.

r001.rationale: The response says AGI has become more contested and describes broadly capable systems, but it does not clearly say that the concept has been watered down as it entered the mainstream.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AGI has always been a somewhat slippery term, and as it’s become more mainstream, people have brought different intuitions to it. Some people mean a system that can do essentially any intellectual task a human can do. Others mean something more like, “This feels broadly intelligent. I can talk to it about almost anything.” Those are pretty different thresholds.

With systems that are already useful across lots of domains, that distinction becomes harder to ignore. You can have this striking breadth of capability alongside failures that seem very basic. So the question “Is it AGI?” can obscure the more useful questions: What can it actually do? How reliably can it do it? How much human supervision does it need?

I tend to find it more helpful to talk about those concrete capabilities and their consequences. A system could have enormous economic or safety implications while people are still arguing about whether it counts as AGI.

r001.rationale: The response says AGI has become more mainstream and that people apply different intuitions and thresholds to it, but it does not say the concept has become more watered down.
